scenarios.title: The Teammate's Party
scenarios.text: A teammate is throwing a party the night before a seven o'clock workout, and the whole rookie class is going. Your phone has been buzzing about it since lunch.

choices.label: Go for an hour
choices.result: An hour of saying hello, then home before ten. Two rookies call you boring in the group chat. In the morning meeting, you're the only one who can keep their eyes open.

choices.label: Sleep instead
choices.result: Nine hours of sleep, and the stories at breakfast are all yours to enjoy secondhand. You feel completely fine about missing them, which surprises you a little.

choices.label: Stay until the end
choices.result: Three in the morning, and you're still there. The workout is a blur, {coach} asks if you're sick, and you tell the truth, which somehow makes it worse.

scenarios.title: The New City
scenarios.text: Two months in {town}, and you've seen the facility, the grocery store and the inside of your apartment. Your blinds have been closed since September.

choices.label: Explore one neighborhood a week
choices.result: A different neighborhood every week, on foot, with no plan. By midseason you know {town} better than some teammates who grew up here, and you have a favorite bakery.

choices.label: Find one place to belong
choices.result: One diner, one gym and one coffee shop, every week, until the people there know your name. It's small, and it's the first time {town} feels like yours.

choices.label: Keep the blinds closed
choices.result: The apartment stays dark between practices. It's restful and easy, and {town} stays a stranger you drive through on the way to work.

scenarios.title: The Family Visit
scenarios.text: {parent} and {sibling} want to visit for a weekend in October. Your schedule doesn't have a weekend in it, and {parent} has already looked up flights and a hotel near the stadium.

choices.label: Make it work
choices.result: The guest room, practice in the morning, every evening with them. You're exhausted by Sunday and happier than you've been in weeks, and {sibling} cries a little at the airport.

choices.label: Ask them to wait for the offseason
choices.result: The offseason, you promise, with a whole week. {parent} understands right away; {sibling} is disappointed and says so, and doesn't text you for a few days.

choices.label: Bring them to practice
choices.result: Two passes to practice and lunch with the team. {sibling} meets the quarterback and talks about it for months, and {parent} keeps the visitor badge on the fridge.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Attention
scenarios.text: Someone recognizes you in the cereal aisle and follows you through three more aisles, talking the whole time about a kick you made in college that you barely remember.

choices.label: Be gracious
choices.result: Stopping costs you ten minutes and a photo by the frozen peas. It makes someone's week, and they post it with a caption about how nice you are.

choices.label: Keep moving, politely
choices.result: A smile, a thank-you and you keep moving. They post that you were 'a little cold', and three people you've never met argue about it for a day.

choices.label: Shop at night
choices.result: Eleven at night becomes your shopping hour. Nobody recognizes you, the cereal aisle is yours alone, and the night cashier starts saving you the good bananas.

scenarios.title: The Local Radio Appearance
scenarios.text: A sports radio show invites you on, live, during drive time. The host is famous for getting rookies to say things, and the producer has warned you there'll be callers.

choices.label: Prepare and go
choices.result: Three stories prepared, all light, and you stick to them. The host can't get anything controversial out of you, laughs anyway and invites you back next month.

choices.label: Wing it
choices.result: No notes. One joke lands beautifully; one answer about the coaching staff gets replayed all week, and {coach} mentions it, dryly, in the next meeting.

choices.label: Spend the hour at the net
choices.result: A polite no, and the hour goes to the kicking net instead. The host makes a joke about shy kickers on air, and you never hear it.

scenarios.title: The Practice Routine
scenarios.text: Your college routine isn't working at this level: too slow for the snapper, too long for the play clock. You need a new one by Sunday, and the veterans are watching to see what you build.

choices.label: Borrow the snapper's rhythm
choices.result: The veteran snapper's pre-kick rhythm becomes yours, step for step. It feels strange for two days, then it feels like it was always yours, and he's quietly proud.

choices.label: Build your own
choices.result: From scratch, charting every kick for a week in a notebook. The new routine is yours entirely, and it holds up when the stadium gets loud.

choices.label: Build it with {coach}
choices.result: {coach} spends an hour with you after practice, building it piece by piece. The coach is clearly pleased you asked, and starts asking your opinion in meetings.

scenarios.title: The First Contract Question
scenarios.text: A reporter asks at your locker whether you expect a contract extension. You haven't kicked a regular-season game yet, and the veteran kicker you replaced is standing two lockers away.

choices.label: Joke about keeping your locker
choices.result: Just trying to keep your locker, you say, and grin. The quote is charming, nobody reads into it, and the veteran two lockers down actually laughs.

choices.label: Say you've earned a look
choices.result: You think you've earned a look, you say. The front office reads it by dinner, and so does the veteran, who stops saying good morning.

choices.label: Leave contracts to your agent
choices.result: Contracts are your agent's job. It's dull and smart, the reporter moves on, and {coach} gives you a small nod across the room.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Struggle
scenarios.text: A fellow rookie is falling apart: late to meetings, quiet at lunch, gone the minute practice ends. Yesterday he forgot his helmet. Nobody's said anything to him yet.

choices.label: Knock on his door
choices.result: His door, after practice, and you stay for an hour. He doesn't say much about what's wrong, but he's early to the next meeting, and he sits next to you.

choices.label: Tell a veteran
choices.result: A veteran you trust hears about it quietly, from you. The veteran handles it better than you could have, and the rookie never finds out who spoke up.

choices.label: Mind your own business
choices.result: Your own roster spot is enough to worry about. He's released a month later, and you think about that empty locker longer than you expected.

scenarios.title: The Family Expectations
scenarios.text: Your family expects more now that you're earning. Cousins call about cars, an uncle about a boat, and {parent} about a roof that's been leaking since you were in high school.

choices.label: Set a family budget
choices.result: A yearly amount for family help, set at the kitchen table with {parent}. It's an awkward hour, and it ends the guessing, and the cousins stop calling about cars.

choices.label: Say yes to everything
choices.result: Yes to every request. It feels wonderful for a month, and your account feels it much longer, and nobody says thank you for the third one.

choices.label: Say not yet
choices.result: A rookie contract isn't forever money, you explain, as patiently as you can. Some of them understand. {sibling} doesn't, and says something you'll both remember.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Bill
scenarios.text: Your car's transmission dies the week before a road trip, in the facility parking lot, in front of the whole offensive line. The repair costs more than the car is worth.

choices.label: Fix it
choices.result: Repaired, and a week of buses to practice in the meantime. The veterans think it's hilarious and start leaving bus schedules in your locker.

choices.label: Buy something new
choices.result: A brand-new car the same afternoon. It's lovely, it smells incredible, and the payment is going to follow you around for years.

choices.label: Ride with a teammate
choices.result: Rides with a teammate until you figure it out, and the drives turn into the best part of your week. By the time your car is fixed, you're friends.

scenarios.title: The Former Coach Calls
scenarios.text: Your old college coach calls on a quiet Wednesday night to check in. After the small talk, there's a pause, and then the question: how are you really doing?

choices.label: Tell the truth
choices.result: Harder than you expected, you admit. Your old coach tells you about every player who said the same thing in their first year, and made it anyway.

choices.label: Say it's great
choices.result: Everything's great, you insist. Your old coach doesn't believe you, says so kindly, and leaves the door open for another call.

choices.label: Ask for help with one thing
choices.result: One specific problem: your timing on short kicks. Your old coach watches your practice film that night and calls back the next morning with an answer.

scenarios.title: The Community Invitation
scenarios.text: A local high school asks you to speak to its athletes about what it takes to make it. The gym will be full, the principal has put your photo on the marquee, and you've never given a speech.

choices.label: Speak honestly
choices.result: The cuts, the doubts, the practice you nearly quit: all of it comes out, simply. Three kids stay after with questions, and one of them is the school's kicker.

choices.label: Run a clinic instead
choices.result: No speech: a kicking clinic on their muddy field instead. Everyone gets filthy, the principal joins in, and the kids remember it better than any speech.

choices.label: Send your regrets
choices.result: The schedule's too full, you explain. They invite a retired linebacker instead, and you see the photos later and wish you'd gone.

scenarios.title: The Dating Question
scenarios.text: Someone you meet at a teammate's dinner party seems much more interested in the league than in you: salaries, famous teammates, whether you can get them into the owner's box.

choices.label: Ask them out anyway
choices.result: The date happens, and they ask a lot about the league and a little about you. You don't call again, and you learn to recognize it faster next time.

choices.label: Change the subject
choices.result: Every time football comes up, you steer away from it. By dessert, they're laughing at your terrible cooking stories, and you realize you're having a good time.

choices.label: Thank the host and go
choices.result: An early thank-you to the host, and you drive home. You'd rather be bored than be someone's résumé, and the drive home is peaceful.
